label: Lecture 12: How It Is Asked
rows: Most questions show the strip: early or late, narrow or wide, and what the P wave looks like.
Any rate in a stem carries the normal resting range (60–100 per minute).
Sawtooth = flutter (“the only rhythm that will have this pattern”); irregularly irregular = fibrillation; no P + narrow + regular + over 150 = supraventricular tachycardia.
No treatment (“solely about rhythm interpretation and diagnosis”). Fibrillation types: “don't get too much into the weeds”.

label: Premature Beats
rows: EARLY, from the atria outside the sinus node (increased automaticity); P wave of NEW SHAPE; narrow QRS.
EARLY, narrow; P wave NONE, INVERTED, or AFTER the QRS. Isolated ones: no clinical significance.
EARLY, WIDE (typically over 0.12 s), NO P wave, T wave OPPOSITE the QRS.
Couplet = 2 · triplet = 3. Same shape = UNIFOCAL (one focus); different shapes = MULTIFOCAL.
Every other beat = BIGEMINY · every 3rd = TRIGEMINY · every 4th = QUADRIGEMINY.
A premature ventricular complex landing on the prior T wave (relative refractory period) can trigger ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.
Frequent or grouped premature ventricular complexes can reduce cardiac output.
Slide 70 says 6 in a row; the usual definition is 3 or more consecutive ventricular beats. A brief (nonsustained) run needs evaluation.

label: Escape Beats & Rhythms
rows: Arrives past the expected R wave, after a pause, because the pacemaker above failed or slowed.
Sinus node fails or slows; late narrow beat; the sinus node then resets.
Escape beats become the rhythm: the atrioventricular node takes over and suppresses the sinus node.
Late and WIDE: BOTH nodes failed.
Named in the objective; no slide in the deck.

label: Junctional Rhythms
rows: Atria first → INVERTED P just before the QRS (short PR). Together → NO P. Ventricles first (trigger zone) → P AFTER the QRS.
REGULAR (an irregular spot = a premature junctional complex); PR under 0.12 s if a P precedes; QRS usually narrow.
TRANSITION = arrhythmogenic, most premature junctional complexes · COMPACT = slows conduction, backup pacemaker · TRIGGER = fires down the His bundle.

label: Idioventricular Rhythms
rows: Purkinje network pacing. 20–40 per minute, REGULAR, WIDE (over 0.12 s), NO P waves.
Junctional: 40–60, P absent or inverted, usually NARROW. Idioventricular: 20–40, no P, WIDE. Both regular.
Slide 75 equates it with idioventricular rhythm; agonal is the very slow (under about 20) dying end.

label: Supraventricular Dysrhythmias
rows: At least 3 P wave shapes, married; IRREGULAR; under 100; PR variable.
The same, OVER 100 per minute (the deck's atrial tachycardia).
Reentry circuit, usually RIGHT atrium (enlarged, scarred, ischemic tissue). SAWTOOTH = pathognomonic. Atrial rate about 300.
Document flutter waves per QRS: 2:1, 3:1. Ratio changing = VARIABLE CONDUCTION (irregular). Count troughs to the next QRS; a notch on the QRS counts.
Many atrial sites, sinus node suppressed, atrial KICK lost. No P waves, fibrillatory waves, IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR, atrial rate indeterminate.
Atrioventricular nodal reentry: REGULAR, NARROW, 150–300, P NOT VISIBLE (or retrograde), started by a premature atrial complex.
Typical: DOWN SLOW, UP FAST; no P or pseudo S waves. Atypical: down fast, up slow; retrograde P clearly visible (RP interval).
Upright sinus P before every QRS at 190 is still SINUS TACHYCARDIA. Unsure P or T? Call it a T wave.
